```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(lme4)
  library(glmmTMB)
  library(emmeans)
  library(DHARMa)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(knitr)
```

## clean data
```{r}
data_file <- "acute_yield_data_fall_2026.csv"
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  data_file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wwy200311gy-sudo/stat628/refs/heads/main/acute_yield_data_fall_2026.csv"
}
d_raw <- read.csv(data_file)

d <- d_raw %>%
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),
    cultivar = factor(toupper(trimws(cultivar))),
    intensity_group = factor(toupper(trimws(intensity_group)),
                               levels = c("D", "C", "B", "A")),
    treatment = factor(toupper(trimws(treatment)),
                               levels = c("CONTROL", "OTC"),
                               labels = c("Control", "OTC")),
    heat_group = factor(
      ifelse(treatment == "Control", "Control", as.character(intensity_group)),
      levels = c("Control", "D", "C", "B", "A")
    ),
    pair = interaction(year, cultivar, intensity_group, plot,
                                    drop = TRUE),
    total_weight = healthy_weight + rotten_weight,
    healthy_count_pct = 100 * healthy_n / (healthy_n + rotten_n),
    healthy_weight_prop = healthy_weight / total_weight,
    healthy_weight_pct  = 100 * healthy_weight_prop,
    pulses = as.numeric(c(A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, D = 1)[
                                      as.character(intensity_group)])
  )

# Design checks -------------------------------------------------------------
stopifnot(nrow(d) == 96, nlevels(d$pair) == 48)
stopifnot(!anyNA(d$heat_group))
stopifnot(all(d %>% count(pair) %>% pull(n) == 2))
stopifnot(all(d %>%
  group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(ok = setequal(as.character(treatment), c("Control", "OTC")),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  pull(ok)))
stopifnot(all(d$total_weight > 0), all(d$healthy_n + d$rotten_n > 0))

```
## model design

Before fitting the models, we use the data to check the modelling choices:
the response scale, the mean-variance relationship, the pair structure, and
which interactions are plausible.

## Response scale

```{r }
d %>%
  transmute(`Total weight (g)` = total_weight,
            `log(total weight)` = log(total_weight)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "scale", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count",
       title = "Total weight on the raw and log scales") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

```{r design-residuals, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Absolute residuals vs fitted values from a Gaussian model. The raw scale shows a mild increase in spread with the fitted value; the log scale is flatter. This supports modelling log(total weight)."}
m_raw <- lm(total_weight ~ heat_group * year + cultivar, data = d)
m_log <- lm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar, data = d)

bind_rows(
  data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_raw), abs_resid = abs(resid(m_raw)),
             scale = "Raw scale"),
  data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_log), abs_resid = abs(resid(m_log)),
             scale = "Log scale")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = abs_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "tomato") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "|Residual|",
       title = "Absolute residuals vs fitted values: raw vs log scale") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

The raw-scale residuals spread out more at high fitted values, while the log-scale
residuals are more even. Together with the positive support, this motivates the
log-normal LMM for total weight.

## Pair structure

```{r design-pairs, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Control and heat total weights within the same pair are strongly correlated (r = 0.84). This supports the pair random intercept (1 | pair)."}
pair_heat <- d %>%
  filter(treatment == "OTC") %>%
  select(pair, heat_group)

wide <- d %>%
  select(pair, treatment, total_weight) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = total_weight,
              id_cols = pair) %>%
  left_join(pair_heat, by = "pair")

cor_pair <- cor(wide$Control, wide$OTC)

ggplot(wide, aes(x = Control, y = OTC, colour = heat_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(D = "#fee5d9", C = "#fcae91",
                                 B = "#fb6a4a", A = "#cb181d")) +
  labs(x = "Control total weight (g)", y = "Heat total weight (g)",
       colour = "Heat group",
       title = sprintf("Within-pair correlation: r = %.2f", cor_pair)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

The within-pair correlation is about 0.84 (and 0.75–0.93 within the four heat
levels). The two plots in a pair are not independent, so the model needs a
`(1 | pair)` random intercept.

## Which interactions are plausible?

```{r design-heat-year, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Mean total weight by heat group and year, separately for each cultivar. The 2024 and 2025 profiles differ: 2025 is lower overall, and MQ declines sharply at B/A in 2025 while ST is flatter. This supports a heat_group x year interaction."}
summ_hy <- d %>%
  group_by(heat_group, year, cultivar) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total_weight),
            se = sd(total_weight) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(summ_hy, aes(x = heat_group, y = mean, colour = year, group = year)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.12) +
  facet_wrap(~ cultivar) +
  labs(x = "Heat group (D = 1, C = 2, B = 3, A = 4 pulses)",
       y = "Mean total weight (g)", colour = "Year",
       title = "Heat group x year, separately by cultivar") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

```{r design-heat-cultivar, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Mean total weight by heat group and cultivar, separately by year. MQ and ST differ mainly in level; their heat profiles are similar enough that a heat_group x cultivar interaction is not obviously required, but it is tested in H1."}
ggplot(summ_hy, aes(x = heat_group, y = mean, colour = cultivar, group = cultivar)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.12) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(x = "Heat group (D = 1, C = 2, B = 3, A = 4 pulses)",
       y = "Mean total weight (g)", colour = "Cultivar",
       title = "Heat group x cultivar, separately by year") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

```{r design-year-cultivar, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Mean total weight by year and cultivar. The large 2025 ST drop supports a year x cultivar baseline term."}
summ_yc <- d %>%
  group_by(year, cultivar) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total_weight),
            se = sd(total_weight) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(summ_yc, aes(x = year, y = mean, colour = cultivar, group = cultivar)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.12) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean total weight (g)", colour = "Cultivar",
       title = "Year x cultivar baseline") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

The figures support the following model structure:

- **log(total_weight)** rather than raw weight: the response is positive, the
  effects are naturally multiplicative, and the log-scale residuals are more
  homogeneous.
- **(1 | pair)**: control and heat plots in the same pair are strongly
  correlated, so the pair must be a random effect.
- **heat_group × year**: the 2024 and 2025 profiles have different shapes,
  especially for MQ; ST is much lower in 2025.
- **year:cultivar**: 2025 ST is much lower than 2024 ST, a baseline shift that
  is not a heat effect.
- **heat_group × cultivar**: MQ and ST differ mainly in level; their heat
  profiles are similar enough that the interaction is tested but not obviously
  required.

The model-building section below fits the candidate models H0–H4 and compares
them with AIC and likelihood-ratio tests.

## model build
```{r}
fit_lmm <- function(form) lmer(form, data = d, REML = FALSE)
# Total weight
h0_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair))

h1_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair))

h2_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar + (1 | pair))

h3_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * (cultivar + year) + year:cultivar + (1 | pair))

h4_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ treatment * intensity_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair))

```
```{r}
aic_tab <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(Response = "Total",   Model = c("H0", "H1", "H2", "H3", "H4"),
             df = sapply(list(h0_total, h1_total, h2_total, h3_total, h4_total),
                         function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
             AIC = sapply(list(h0_total, h1_total, h2_total, h3_total, h4_total), AIC)),
) %>%
  group_by(Response) %>%
  mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC)) %>%
  ungroup()
kable(aic_tab)

```

We can choose h2_total, which has the smallest AIC. 

We refit the selected H2 model with REML for the final estimates:

```{r h2-formula}
h2_final <- lmer(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar +
                   (1 | pair), data = d, REML = TRUE)

formula(h2_final)
```

$$
\log Y_i=\mu+\alpha_{g_i}+\beta_{t_i}+(\alpha\beta)_{g_i t_i}
+\gamma_{c_i}+(\beta\gamma)_{t_i c_i}+b_{k(i)}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad b_k\sim N(0,\sigma_b^2),\quad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2),
$$

where $Y_i$ is `total_weight` (g), $g_i$ is the heat group, $t_i$ the year and
$c_i$ the cultivar. The reference levels are Control, 2024 and MQ, so the
heat-group coefficients are log ratios relative to Control in 2024 for MQ, and
the `:year2025` terms add the extra change in 2025.

## Coefficients of the selected H2 model

```{r h2-coefficients}
h2_coef <- summary(h2_final)$coefficients

h2_coef_tab <- data.frame(
  term         = rownames(h2_coef),
  estimate     = h2_coef[, "Estimate"],
  std_error    = h2_coef[, "Std. Error"],
  t_value      = h2_coef[, "t value"],
  p_value      = format.pval(2 * pnorm(-abs(h2_coef[, "t value"])),
                             digits = 3, eps = 1e-4),
  exp_estimate = exp(h2_coef[, "Estimate"]),
  lower_95     = exp(h2_coef[, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * h2_coef[, "Std. Error"]),
  upper_95     = exp(h2_coef[, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * h2_coef[, "Std. Error"]),
  row.names    = NULL
)

kable(h2_coef_tab, digits = 4,
      col.names = c("Term", "Estimate (log)", "SE", "t", "p",
                    "exp(Estimate)", "95% lower", "95% upper"))
```

How to read the rows:

- `(Intercept)`: log mean total weight for Control, 2024, MQ.
- `heat_groupD`, `heat_groupC`, `heat_groupB`, `heat_groupA`: log ratio of that
  heat group to Control in 2024 (MQ); `exp(Estimate)` is the ratio.
- `year2025`: log ratio 2025/2024 for Control, MQ.
- `cultivarST`: log ratio ST/MQ for Control, 2024.
- `heat_groupX:year2025`: extra log ratio in 2025, so the 2025 heat ratio is
  `exp(heat_groupX + heat_groupX:year2025)`.
- `year2025:cultivarST`: extra ST/MQ change in 2025.

## Variance components

```{r h2-variance}
h2_vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(h2_final))
sigma2_pair  <- h2_vc$vcov[h2_vc$grp == "pair"]
sigma2_resid <- h2_vc$vcov[h2_vc$grp == "Residual"]

h2_var_tab <- data.frame(
  component = c("pair variance", "residual variance",
                "pair SD", "residual SD", "ICC"),
  value     = c(sigma2_pair,
                sigma2_resid,
                sqrt(sigma2_pair),
                sqrt(sigma2_resid),
                sigma2_pair / (sigma2_pair + sigma2_resid))
)

kable(h2_var_tab, digits = 4)
```

## Predicted total weight by heat group, year and cultivar

```{r h2-predicted, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Predicted total weight (g) by heat group, year and cultivar, with pointwise 95% confidence intervals from the H2 model."}
pred_grid <- expand.grid(
  heat_group = levels(d$heat_group),
  year       = levels(d$year),
  cultivar   = levels(d$cultivar),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pred_grid$heat_group <- factor(pred_grid$heat_group, levels = levels(d$heat_group))
pred_grid$year       <- factor(pred_grid$year, levels = levels(d$year))
pred_grid$cultivar   <- factor(pred_grid$cultivar, levels = levels(d$cultivar))

pred_fit <- predict(h2_final, newdata = pred_grid, re.form = NA, se.fit = TRUE)
pred_grid$fit   <- exp(pred_fit$fit)
pred_grid$lower <- exp(pred_fit$fit - 1.96 * pred_fit$se.fit)
pred_grid$upper <- exp(pred_fit$fit + 1.96 * pred_fit$se.fit)

p_pred <- ggplot(pred_grid, aes(x = heat_group, y = fit, group = 1)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.15, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_grid(cultivar ~ year) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(Control = "Control", D = "D (1)", C = "C (2)",
                              B = "B (3)", A = "A (4)")) +
  labs(
    x = "Heat group",
    y = "Predicted total weight (g)",
    title = "Predicted total weight by heat group, year and cultivar",
    subtitle = "H2 model; fixed-effect predictions with 95% confidence intervals",
    caption = "Intervals are pointwise and back-transformed from the log scale."
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

p_pred
```

Overall, heat stress reduces total fruit weight, but how much it reduces depended on the year and the number of pulses. Averaged over A–D, the reduction is about 11.5% (95% CI 6.6–16.2%, p < 0.001). In 2024 the reduction is smaller, about 7.8% (p = 0.038); after Holm adjustment, none of the individual heat levels is significantly different from Contro. In 2025 the reduction is larger, about 15.1% (p < 0.001), with A (4 pulses) down 36.9% and B (3 pulses) down 18.7%, while C and D are close to Control. Overall A has the largest effect about −25.9%.

The figure shows a similar pattern: from Control to A, as the number of pulses goes from 0 to 4, total weight generally goes down. In 2024, MQ and ST has similar curves and differed mainly in level. in 2025, ST drops a lot while MQ only decreases a little. This suggests that the year effect matters more for ST, which may also mean that MQ is more stable. But the model did not find a heat*cultivar interaction (p = 0.28); MQ and ST differ mainly in baseline, and the 2025 ST baseline is much lower than in 2024.
